THOUGHT: This patient has hyperthermia (41.1°C), profound tachycardia (HR 170), altered mental status, diaphoresis, and a history of known hyperthyroidism treated with propranolol and a recent surgical stressor — a constellation most consistent with thyrotoxic crisis (thyroid storm). Thyroid storm commonly presents with fever, delirium/AMS, marked sympathetic overactivity including tachyarrhythmia (often atrial fibrillation with RVR), and profuse sweating; it is typically precipitated by surgery, infection, or other stressors. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is less likely because NMS usually causes “lead‑pipe” rigidity and develops over days after dopamine blockade (this patient has minimal muscle tone, not rigidity). Serotonin syndrome would show neuromuscular hyperactivity (hyperreflexia, clonus) and requires serotonergic agents (none documented). Malignant hyperthermia is tightly temporally linked to anesthesia exposure (minutes–hours), not months later. Sepsis could present similarly but the presence of known hyperthyroidism, recent surgical stress, and extreme tachyarrhythmia favors thyroid storm as the most likely unifying diagnosis.

DIAGNOSIS: Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis)
